They're not the same. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive only reuses one TCP connection for requests one after another, so each request waits for the previous response and browsers open several connections to get parallelism. HTTP/2 multiplexing interleaves many concurrent request and response streams as frames over a single connection, though TCP-level head-of-line blocking is still there (HTTP/3 fixes that).

AsyncLocalStorage keeps data tied to an async call chain, so you can set a request id once and read it in the logger or any deep function without passing it as an argument. The overhead is small but not zero, so measure it on hot paths. It fits our request-id gap well.

Use a Deployment for stateless pods that are interchangeable, so any pod can be replaced or scaled freely. Pick a StatefulSet when each pod needs a stable identity and storage: stable names and DNS (pod-0, pod-1), ordered start and rollout, and its own persistent volume per replica, as for databases or clustered brokers.

structuredClone keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays, undefined and circular references. The JSON round trip turns Dates into strings, Maps and Sets into {}, drops undefined and functions, and throws on cycles. Neither copies functions or class prototypes.
